questions.question: When is 'sample several answers and check them' a good strategy?
options: When checking an answer is cheaper and more reliable than producing it
questions.explanation: Scheduling, code with tests, SQL and plans all fit this shape.

questions.question: Why did majority vote get worse as N grew?
options: The time-zone mistake was the single most common answer, so more samples made it win more reliably
questions.explanation: Voting amplifies systematic errors; it only helps when errors are scattered.

questions.question: With an exact checker and per-sample success p, what is the chance at least one of N samples is valid?
questions.explanation: With p = 0.35 and N = 10: 98.7%, matching the simulation's 98.2%.

questions.question: Why did the judged strategy plateau near 66%?
options: The judge wrongly accepts invalid answers 30% of the time, and more samples don't remove that
questions.explanation: An imperfect verifier sets a ceiling; measure its false-accept rate.

questions.question: Why does verify() return reasons instead of True/False?
options: So the same checker can give feedback to a reviser or planner, and say why a slot fails
questions.explanation: Reasons connect verification to repair (Lessons 2 and 5).

questions.question: The offline proposer's error rates were chosen by the author. What does that mean for the table?
options: The numbers are measurements of a model
The table shows the mechanism under stated assumptions; your model's rates must be measured (e.g. with --live)
questions.explanation: A simulation shows effects; it doesn't measure any real model.
